## Understanding the system behind the measurements
When studying the neurobiological effects of depression or its treatment, we need to recognize that 
the changes we measure in the brain are representations of a much more complex underlying phenomenon. 
Brain structure and function are influenced by an interplay of genetic, environmental, biological, 
and psychological factors. Neuroimaging methods such as MRI, PET, and MEG/EEG provide different 
perspectives on this system, allowing us to observe particular aspects of its behaviour. 
However, these measurements do not necessarily reveal the underlying mechanisms responsible for that behaviour.

### Observing patterns versus understanding mechanisms
An analogy can be made to playing a video game. A person can become highly skilled at a game by learning 
its rules, recognizing patterns, and understanding how different actions produce different outcomes. 
Yet, this does not mean that they understand the programming, algorithms, or hardware that make the game possible. 
They understand how to interact with the system, but not necessarily how the system works at a deeper level.

Similarly, in neuroscience, we can become very skilled at identifying patterns in neuroimaging data, describing changes, 
and establishing associations between brain measures and clinical outcomes. However, this does not automatically mean 
that we understand the underlying biological mechanisms.

Perhaps we need to remain conscious of this distinction: we are observing the behaviour of a complex system through 
different measurement techniques, rather than directly accessing or fully understanding the system itself. 
Our task is not only to describe what changes, but to gradually understand why and how those changes occur. We need to 
be aware of what we can and cannot say anything about and what questions we are and are not able to answer.
